segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's this moment during the Cuban Missile Crisis that's so incredible, it doesn't sound real. But we have confirmed this with people who were there. Victor Gilinsky wrote about this for the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He said, basically, nuclear war seemed so imminent that the underground headquarters of the Strategic Air Command in Nebraska went into lock down. Nobody was allowed to enter or leave. He said the General in charge told the staff he expected an order to launch nuclear missiles any moment, and also expected that they would all die from a Soviet counterattack.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And everybody was allowed to make one phone call home to their family. But in that call, they were not allowed to say why they were calling. What do you say in that situation?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Gilinsky writes, "The conversations were about scraped kids' knees and sick dogs. It was a scene straight out of Dr. Strangelove ." And of course, right? What can words do when you're staring death in the face?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, today on our program, we have two stories where ordinary people rise to this exact task. They see death standing there, and they open their mouths. And truly amazing things happen.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We have two stories for you today. And to say anything else about these stories, I think, would be a spoiler. Also, I want to give every possible second to these stories. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. And let's just get to it with the first act of our show.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So remember that tsunami that hit Japan five years ago, March 2011? Giant black waves more than 30-feet tall hit Japan.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: A guy in a little town called Otsuchi shot this video. You can hear him yelling.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: All the houses are washing away.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Otsuchi had been there for 100 years. In 30 minutes, it was gone-- almost totally flattened.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The tsunami and the earthquake that went with it killed six times more people than died in 9/11-- over 19,000 people. Another 2,500 are still missing. And in the aftermath, of course, families struggled to figure out how they were going to move forward without the people they loved.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And in that town of Otsuchi, it lead to this new-- I don't know, ritual is not exactly the right word for this. But it's something close to that-- this thing that people invented to stay connected to the dead. One of our producers, Miki Meek, has family in Japan.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And she grew up going back and forth between there and here. And she watched this documentary about this thing people are doing Otsuchi, on the Japanese news channel, NHK, and got permission for us to play you some excerpts. Here's Miki.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Of all the areas in Japan affected by that tsunami, Otsuchi has one of the highest numbers of missing people-- 421. Today, it's still partly in ruins and partly a construction site, as they try to rebuild the town on higher ground. But a year before that tsunami happened, this guy named Itaru Sasaki-- he was already dealing with a loss.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: His cousin had just died. And Itaru was having a hard time figuring out how to talk about it. So he did something pretty ingenious.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: He went out and bought an old-fashioned phone booth and stuck it in his garden. It looks like an old English-style one. It's square and painted white, and has these glass window panes.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Inside is a black rotary phone, resting on a wood shelf. This phone connected to nowhere. It didn't work at all.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: But that didn't matter to Itaru. He just needed a place where he felt like he could talk to his cousin, a place where he could air out his grief. And so putting an old phone booth in his garden, which sits on this little windy hill overlooking the Pacific Ocean, it felt like a perfect solution.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: He's saying, because my thoughts could not be relayed over a regular phone line, I wanted them to be carried on the wind.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: So I named it the wind telephone-- kaze no denwa. The idea of keeping up a relationship with the dead is not such a strange one in Japan. The line between our world and their world is thin.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Lots of families keep a Buddhist altar for their dead relatives in the living room. My uncle has one for our family. There are photos on a little platform. And every day, he leaves fresh fruit and rice for them, lights incense, and rings a bell. It's a way to stay in touch, to let them know that they're still a big part of our family.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: So after the tsunami and earthquake happened, word got out about Itaru's special wind telephone-- that he was using it as another way to stay connected to the dead. Soon, people started showing up randomly on his property, and walking right into the phone booth. This has been going on for five years now. Itaru estimates that thousands of people from all over Japan have come to use his phone.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: A TV station asked Itaru, and the people who come to use his phone, if they could videotape their calls from a distance, and put an audio recorder in the phone booth. They wanted to get a sense of how people are still grieving. I watched their documentary after the fifth anniversary of the tsunami back in March. That whole week, all of the news programs in Japan were airing memorial programs.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: But I found the calls in this particular program remarkable and moving, for just how simple they were. One woman from Otsuchi, named Sachiko Okawa, showed up one afternoon. She's 71-years-old, and lost her husband in the tsunami.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: She regularly brings her two young grandsons to the phone booth. And you can tell, by how casually they talk to him on the phone. They squish into the phone booth with their grandma, wearing matching blue-and-black-striped shirts.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Sachiko starts the call by picking up the receiver and saying hello.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Her oldest grandson quickly jumps in.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I'll be in fourth grade next semester. Wasn't that fast?

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Daina, my younger brother, he'll be in second grade next year. Then Sachiko corrects him. She says, no, Daina will be in second grade this year, not next.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: A lot of calls were just like this, straightforward updates about life. The kind of a quick highlights reel you might give to any family member you were catching up with on the phone. The boy, he then tells his grandpa--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I'm giving the phone to Daina now.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Daina, his little brother, grabs the phone.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Grandpa, I finished all my homework. Sachiko urges him to keep talking.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: He says, everyone is doing fine. Then he hangs up. They all say goodbye.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: As they're walking out of the booth, Daina says--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Maybe Grandpa will say  he heard us.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: In another call, a woman in a puffy winter jacket with a fur-lined hood shows up at the booth by herself. Her name is Kikue Hirano, and she's 66. She used to live in Otsuchi. But she moved away after she lost her house and her husband in the tsunami.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Her husband was a deep-sea fisherman. His name was Miyoji, and they used to talk and drink sake together at night. Now Kikue lives alone, about 50 miles away.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: But sometimes Kikue finds herself driving back to Otsuchi, into this booth. I watched her do this thing that a lot of callers seem to do. You hear Kikue actually dialing the rotary phone--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: 4, 2, 5, 7, 4, 4. She's dialing the phone number for her old house in Otsuchi, the last place she knew to reach her husband. Then Kikue just stands in the booth in silence, holding the phone to her ear.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Sometimes she fidgets around and tilts her head up, and concentrates on the ceiling, the same way I do when I want to cry but I'm trying hard not to. It doesn't work. Kikue brushes some tears off her face. Eventually, she hangs up.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: She lingers in the booth a little longer, hands clasped together in front of her, staring at the phone booth floor. She walks out. One pattern that the owner of the phone booth, Itaru, has noticed over the years is that more men than women come to use it. Not surprisingly, this is not a demographic that's known for sharing their feelings, especially the older farmers. They already have a reputation for not talking much.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: In one of the phone calls recorded in winter, a man with gray hair and a little towel hanging around his neck walks into the garden. This kind of towel is part of the uniform of Japanese farmers. They use them to wipe away sweat and clean their hands.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: This man opens the telephone booth door. And under his breath, you hear him say, huh, so this is the wind telephone? This appears to be his very first visit to the phone booth.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: He lost his oldest son in the tsunami. His son's name was Nobuyuki. He also lost his house, and had to move into temporary housing with his wife.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: And recently, she got sick and also passed away. He calls her okaasan. It means "mom" in Japanese. It's what everyone in the family calls the female head of the house, even the husband. It's a very intimate, loving term.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Sorry to ask this, but take care of her, and your grandma and grandpa too.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He uses the towel around his neck to wipe his eyes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One of the things that makes these calls so poignant to me is all the understated ways that people are actually saying, I love you, and I miss you. I'd never say something so direct like that in Japanese. It's just not done.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I've only seen people say it in the soap operas. [JAPANESE]. Even saying that right now, it feels weird. I've never said that to my mom or my grandparents.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Take this call. It's winter. The phone booth is surrounded by snow.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Where are you? He's an older man wearing a baseball cap. He also calls his wife "mom." His wife, daughter, and mother, they all went missing in the tsunami.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: It's so cold. But you're not getting cold, are you?

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Are grandma and our daughter, Miyuki, with you too?

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Be found soon. Everyone is waiting for you.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I'll build the house in the same place.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He never says I love you directly. Real feelings are communicated through small gestures, especially ones of concern. Like when he asked his wife, are you staying warm?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Are you eating? And then promising, I'll build a house for us. These are total heartfelt declarations of love.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: For other men, the phone booth is a place where they can finally say their complicated feelings out loud. They can voice their regrets. Anyone who's had someone close to them die knows this feeling.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Like, I've kept having the same one-way conversation with my dad in my head, ever since he passed away last year. I just keep telling him all the situations where I wish I had been kinder, more patient. One call I watched was from a young father, with rectangle glasses and a long black jacket.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: He lost his family-- both parents, his wife-- her name was Mine-- and one-year-old son, named Issei.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: It's already been five years since the disaster.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: If this voice reaches you, please listen.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Sometimes I don't know what I'm living for.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Issei, please let me hear you call me Papa.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Even though I built a new house--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I want to hear your reply, but I can't hear anything.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: He hangs up the phone, takes off his glasses, and covers his eyes with his hands.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I'm so sorry I couldn't save you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's a couple phrases I heard callers tell the dead, again and again. Shinpai shina, don't worry about us. And ganbatteiru, which basically means, I'm doing my very best. I'm enduring.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In Japan, ganbatteiru-- it's a catchall slogan for slogging through life's many challenges, no matter how tiny or big. From trying to pass a test at school, to grieving, you hear it all the time for everything. In the phone booth, ganbatteiru, and shinpai shina-- these are key phrases to reassure the dead that the living, the people left behind, they're doing OK, even if they're not.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: People don't want to worry or burden their loved ones, even dead loved ones. Because most Japanese are Buddhist, and generally believe that when someone dies, they're not suddenly relieved of all their earthly concerns. They're not automatically in heaven, happy and carefree. Many people believe that if the dead see a family member suffering, they can't let go of their earthly life. They hesitate to cross to the other side, and end up stuck in a no-man's land.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I heard these reassurances in a call from a 15-year-old kid named Ren Kozaki, to his dad. He arrived at the phone booth after spending four hours on public transportation by himself. Ren lives in a city much farther north that wasn't affected as much by the tsunami.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But his dad was a truck driver who drove all over Japan. And in a last-minute schedule change, he got sent on a route that took him along the coast when the tsunami hit. He's been missing ever since. Ren went into the phone booth wearing a red backpack.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And what he does in his call-- you hear him signaling to his dad that it's OK. He should keep moving on into the after world.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: The four of us are doing fine.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: You don't need to worry about us. Shinpai shina.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I do have one question I want to ask you.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Why did you die? Why did it have to be you, dad?

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Why am I the only one who is different from everyone else?

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: They never found anything of you.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I wanted to talk with you again.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Ren left the booth. In late February, he came back with his entire family-- his mom, younger brother, and sister. They all drove down to Otsuchi together. And when they got to the phone booth, at first, they kind of awkwardly hung out in front of it. So to break the ice, Ren walks in and places the first call to their dad. He tells him--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I brought everyone with me today.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Bye. When Ren walks out, his family laughs. They say--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: --that was so fast. Ren shoots back--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: It was just a quick report to Dad, that I brought everyone with me today. Next up are Ren's little brother and sister, who are 12 and 14 years old.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: They go into the booth together. And the sister is talking and laughing nervously.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: What am I supposed to say? What should I tell them?

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Wait, wait, don't leave me alone in here.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: The sister picks up the phone. And let me just say, the mom told the film crew that this is a girl who has not said a single word about her dad to anyone since he went missing five years ago. So she picks up the phone and starts to cry.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: She asks her brother again, when should I talk to him about? Her little brother's name is Riku, and he tells her--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Say what you wanted to tell him.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Are you trying to make me laugh, Riku? Riku says--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Then she finally starts talking to her dad. The conversation is all over the place, and she's crying so hard, she can barely talk.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Dad, I'm so sorry I always used to say you were stinky.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: What happen to your promise to buy me a violin?

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Now I'll have to buy one myself.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Her little brother, who sticks close to her, he encourages her to keep going. He says--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: What else? So she tells her dad--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I started tennis in junior high school. I'm not in the top eight.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I want to be in the top eight our last tournament.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I got hooked on this boy band, the Johnnys, when I was in my first year of junior high. I'm still hooked.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: --goodbye. They come out of the booth together.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Now it's their mom's turn. Her kids tell her, itterashai.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Good luck. Ren, the oldest, he bows and waves to her. She walks in, picks up the phone, and lets out a big sigh.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I feel like you're still alive-- somewhere.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: We had so many things we wanted to do together.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Over the phone, we always said to each other, are you alive? Yes, I'm alive.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: It was our password between the two of us, wasn't it?

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: I can't ask you that anymore.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: We, all four of us together, we will be waiting.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: After she comes out, the family lingers outside the phone booth for a while.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This was literally the first time they'd all talked about their dad together, since the tsunami happened five years ago. The youngest, Riku-- he sat quietly on a bench, with his head in his hands. The night before his dad disappeared, they went to a public bath together. His mom and older siblings tell him--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Riku, you don't need to keep your feelings in. Go ahead and cry when you want to. Ren, the oldest, gently teases him. He says--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: See? He can't stop crying. Mom says yeah, but--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: It's OK, because you held back. You endured until now.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: The sister then hands Riku her handkerchief.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: The mom says her kids, we were all about to fall apart. We were so broken. We didn't think we could make it through. And maybe that's why we never talked about dad until now. But talking to him on the phone today, it changed something.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Miki Meek is one of the producers of our program. Thanks to NHK Sendai, who recorded all this, and shared it with us. Coming up, two brothers in their 80s have a last chance to talk to each other before they die. And neither wants to take it. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio, when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's program-- "One Last Thing Before I Go," stories that are about-- well, they're about what power do words have in the face of death? We've arrived at Act Two of our program.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act Two, Uncle's Keeper. So in the first act of our program, people kind of defied death by making small talk-- and some talk that was not so small-- with their dead relatives.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In this act, somebody wants to do something very similar-- make a connection that seemed impossible between people. Except in this story, all the relatives are alive, which you'd think would make it super easy. This story comes from Jonathan Goldstein.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: This is my father, Buzz. I'm calling him at his home in Montreal. And the reason we're talking crazy talk is because it's Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, which seems as good a day as any to talk with him about forgiveness.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: I wanted to ask you something. And I just wanted to gauge your interest.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: How-- how would you feel about paying your brother Sheldon a visit?

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: I have no feelings about it. I'm not really interested.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: My father, Buzz, is 80. And his brother, Sheldon, his only sibling, is 85. And for the past 40 years, they've pretty much been on the outs.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: My father lives in Montreal, and Sheldon lives in Florida. And the last time they saw each other, over 20 years ago, was at their mother's funeral, where they had a fight over the details of the arrangements. Since then, they've hardly spoken.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: It worries me, because there's not a lot of time left. And I don't want my father to have regrets. And my father has a profound capacity for regret. My mother gave up trying to reunite them years ago, after many attempts. So I know that if I don't push him, no one else will.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: I'm not surprised that you're not jumping at the idea. But I'm a little surprised--

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: -- that you're as against the idea.

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: Yeah, time's passed. He hasn't shown much interest. So I'm respecting that, and I leave him alone.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: What he did do, was he called you on your 80th birthday, not so long ago.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: And you felt good about that.

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: Yeah, because I called him on his 80th birthday.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: This kind of tit-for-tat accounting is what always gets in the way.

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: You know what it is at this point, with him? I'll tell you what it is. I don't think it's even anger. He's past anger, and he's past any feelings of animosity. He's past that. He just doesn't care.

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: You know, that's apathy. I mean, sometimes-- at least hate or love, they're emotions. Apathy is nothing.

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: But you know what? Jonny, as a child, even when I was 10, when I was 9 and 8, I was crazy about him. We had a great-- you know, I loved him. He was the older brother. He was-- hello?

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: You know, I just looked up to him. And he had all the friends. Sometimes he'd take me along with him. And he was [AUDIO OUT]. [INAUDIBLE]. Somebody tried-- is somebody to call here, binging me here?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: The most complicated question, the one I keep coming back to, is how did the bad blood begin? And there are many versions. An ill-fated trip to Montreal, where Sheldon felt slighted about having to stay in my father's basement. An ill-fated trip to New York, where my father felt slighted about having to stay in Sheldon's attic.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Rude words spoken to each other's wives. In one version of the story, Sheldon's refusal to bring a table to my bris almost resulted in my being circumcised on an ironing board. But in the version being told today, my father was asked by Sheldon to pay more than his fair share for their mother's funeral.

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: And I said, you're always working some kind of an angle. So he got furious. He got furious. He started screaming into the phone, go to hell. Drop dead, bah, bah, bah. He was-- that was how that ended.

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: But I feel he's the kind of guy, that he has angles like that, you know? He has angles. I always felt I was on the up-and-up with him, and he wasn't with me.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: If you got a stronger sense that he was interested in seeing you, then would you--

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: You would be more inclined to see him?

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: I wouldn't stay at his house though, that's out of the question.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: OK, quick sidebar. Anytime I've ever raised the prospect of visiting Sheldon, no matter how hypothetical the scenario, my father always makes a point of insisting how no matter what, he would not stay in Sheldon's house-- even if he was invited to. Which, I should point out, he never is.

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: I wouldn't stay at his house.

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: I wouldn't stay there. I mean, it's not my thing.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: How come you always bring that up?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: Normally, when someone goes to visit someone that they haven't seen in decades, they'll stay at a hotel, you know? [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: I would stay at a motel or somewhere near his place.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: [LAUGHS] A motel. Yeah, no, we'd get a place with an ice machine and-- you know.

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: Why, you're interested in making a trip?

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
segments.text: I'm interested-- [SIGHS] Do you think that there's anything to be gained in seeing him?

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: Hmm, I guess there's something. You share your common experience, and you talk about the old days. There are things that only he and I can remember. You know?

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: What you could do is, you could call him.

segments.speaker: Buzz Goldstein
segments.text: And see what his attitude is. You know? It depends on how you feel, what kind of reception you get.

segments.speaker: Jonathan Goldstein
